Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-10-20](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-10-20).

The 285 majors in the data fall into broad fields, and 14 of those fields have 8 or more majors.
The table puts them in order of AI exposure.
Engineering Tech sits lowest, with a median exposure percentile of 14, and Interdisciplinary sits highest, at 81.

Pay does not follow.
Across all 285 majors, starting salary and AI exposure have a correlation of 0.005, which is close to none.
The fields show it as well.
Every one of the 17 Engineering Tech majors and the 38 Engineering majors starts above the all-majors median of $41,189, and their fields sit at 14 and 55.
All 10 Visual & Performing Arts majors start below it, and their field sits at an exposure percentile of 20.
The other 11 fields have majors on both sides of the dashed line.

Within a field, high and low exposure are mixed along the salary axis.
In 11 of the 14 fields, the majors include some below and some above the 50th percentile of exposure, and they sit side by side in the strip.
This is a different set of 11 from the one above: Agriculture, Visual & Performing Arts and Foreign Languages are the three fields without that mix.
The link between the two has no fixed direction: inside a field it is positive in 9 fields and negative in 5.
It reaches 0.64 in Visual & Performing Arts and minus 0.63 in Architecture, but with 8 to 38 majors per field, each of these correlations is unreliable.

Some cautions.
AI exposure measures how much a job overlaps with what AI can do, not whether the job will be lost.
Salaries are pooled medians across institutions, and the exposure of a major is the mean over the occupations that the CIP-to-SOC crosswalk links to it.
One year after graduation is early in a career, so these salaries say little about where each field ends up.
